exception: Ends in -er but is not an agent noun (window), so it falls outside this rule and is neuter instead.
A non-agentive -er word (mother) that is feminine, showing the rule only reliably applies to true agent/doer nouns.
Common -er noun (water) that is neuter, not an agent noun.
A loanword (ship's railing) from Dutch/English that happens to end in -ling but is feminine — one of the few genuine exceptions.
A native German word (gate/goal) that happens to end in -or but is neuter, not a Latin loanword.
Short for Laboratorium; neuter despite the -or ending.
Moor (bog/moorland) is neuter, not masculine, despite ending in -or.
Virus is neuter in standard German despite the -us ending — one of the best-known everyday exceptions to this rule.
Plus (an advantage, a 'plus point') is neuter, not masculine, despite ending in -us.
Minus (a deficit/shortfall) is neuter, not masculine, despite ending in -us.
French loanword ending in -ant that is neuter, not an agent noun.
Another French food loanword ending in -ant that is neuter rather than masculine.
Looks like it ends in -eur but is actually the unrelated native word Aben-teuer (adventure); neuter.
French loanword (color/character, used for fraternity colors) that is feminine rather than masculine.
The year itself is neuter, even though it belongs to the calendar-units family.
The week is feminine, unlike the masculine day and month names.
Night is feminine, not masculine, despite belonging to the time-of-day family.
An alternative word for 'spring' that is neuter, contrasting with the standard masculine der Frühling.
Sunshine is feminine, not masculine, despite being a common weather word.
Cloud is feminine, breaking the weather-is-masculine tendency.
Ice is neuter, not masculine.
Thunderstorm is neuter; the general word das Wetter (weather) itself is also neuter.
Beer is the single most famous exception to the 'alcoholic drinks are masculine' rule; it is neuter.
A wine/fruit punch is feminine because it follows the common '-e ending is usually feminine' pattern instead.
The nickname for the Citroën 2CV ('duck') is feminine because it follows the everyday word Ente, not the car-brand rule.
'Member' is neuter regardless of the person's sex — grammatical gender doesn't always track the referent's sex.
'Child' is neuter regardless of sex.
'Person' is grammatically feminine no matter who is being referred to, including men.
'Genius' is neuter despite the -ie ending.
Hippie is masculine, not feminine, despite the -ie ending — an English loanword referring to a person, similar to der Yuppie.
Refers to a male Catholic person, so it is masculine rather than following the -ik-is-feminine pattern.
'Appointment' ends in -in but is an unrelated masculine word, not a feminine-agent form.
French loanword ending in -in that is neuter, unrelated to the feminizing suffix.
'Ruby' ends in -in but is masculine — the ending here is coincidental, not the feminizing suffix.
The school-leaving exam is neuter despite the -ur ending.
Schwur (an oath/vow) is masculine, not feminine, despite the -ur ending.
'Hallway/corridor' is masculine, a common everyday exception to the -ur pattern.
'Cheese' ends in -e but is masculine.
'Eye' ends in -e but is neuter.
'End' ends in -e but is neuter.
'Boy' ends in -e but is masculine, matching natural gender rather than the suffix pattern.
'Interest' ends in -e but is neuter.
Apple is masculine — it ends in -el, which pulls it into the masculine -el pattern instead.
Maple is one of the best-known masculine tree exceptions.
Dandelion is masculine, not feminine.
Poppy is masculine.
Lilac is masculine, ending in -er like many masculine nouns.
The Rhine, one of the most important German rivers, is masculine, not feminine.
The Main river is masculine.
The Neckar river is masculine.
'Girl' is neuter, not feminine, because the diminutive suffix -chen always overrides natural gender and forces neuter.
The old-fashioned word for 'young lady/miss' is neuter for the same reason: the -lein diminutive suffix forces neuter.
An old/blunt word for 'woman' that is neuter rather than feminine, an irregular historical holdover.
'Consumption' is masculine despite the -um ending.
Meaning 'a point in time,' this common word is masculine (das Moment exists separately with the more technical meaning 'factor/momentum').
'Cement' is masculine, not neuter.
'Wealth' is masculine, one of the two best-known exceptions to the -tum-is-neuter pattern.
'Error/mistake' is masculine, the other well-known exception.
'Thought' is masculine, not neuter, despite the Ge- prefix.
'Taste' is masculine, an exception to the Ge-is-neuter pattern.
'Danger' is feminine despite starting with Ge-.
'View/sight' ends in -icht but is feminine.
'Duty' ends in -icht but is feminine.
The currency name is masculine despite ending in -o.
The Italian coffee loanword is masculine.
This Spanish food loanword ending in -o is feminine, not neuter.
'Company/firm' ends in -ma but is feminine, one of the best-known exceptions.
This loanword ends in -ma but is masculine, not neuter.
'Knowledge' ends in -nis but is feminine, part of the large feminine minority in this group.
'Permission' ends in -nis but is feminine.
'Realization/insight' ends in -nis but is feminine.
'Wilderness' ends in -nis but is feminine.
Steel (technically an alloy, not a pure element) is masculine.
Bronze (an alloy) is feminine, following the -e ending pattern instead.
Sulfur is masculine, ending in -el like many masculine nouns.
Phosphorus is masculine, following the -or ending pattern instead of the metals/elements pattern.
Switzerland is feminine and always used with the article, unlike most countries.
Turkey is feminine and always takes an article, like other countries ending in -ei.
Iran is masculine and always takes an article.
Iraq is masculine and always takes an article.
Used only in the plural (die Vereinigten Staaten), unlike the singular neuter default for most countries.
'Puppy' is masculine, not neuter, despite naming a baby animal.
'Larva/grub' (an immature insect) is feminine, not neuter.
The generic word for 'letter' (as in 'a letter of the alphabet') is itself masculine, not neuter.
